title: Give Up Gracefully
summary: Slow dependencies are worse than dead ones. Timeouts, careful retries, circuit breakers, fallbacks and bulkheads keep one failure from spreading.

goals.text: Set timeouts so slow calls can't hold every thread
Retry with backoff and jitter without starting a storm
Stop calling a failing service with a circuit breaker
Degrade with fallbacks and isolate with bulkheads
Propagate deadlines down the call chain

steps.title: A checkout with two helpers
body: Hearth delivers groceries. When a shopper checks out, the Orders service asks Payments to charge the card and asks Picks for “you may also like” suggestions to show on the confirmation page.
Orders handles requests with a pool of 200 worker threads. On a normal evening only a handful are busy at once.

steps.title: Slow is worse than down
body: The payments database's disk saturates and queries slow to many seconds. Payments doesn't fail — it just answers slowly. Orders' HTTP client has the default timeout of 60 seconds, so every checkout thread waits.
Within seconds all 200 threads are stuck. Orders can't even serve requests that don't need Payments. One slow dependency has spread into a full outage: a cascading failure.

callout.text: A dead service fails fast and frees resources. A slow one holds them. Every remote call needs a timeout.

card.title: No timeout set
lines: the HTTP client's default: wait 60 s
each stuck call holds an Orders thread
! Orders stops answering anything at all

steps.title: Decide how long to wait
body: Set an explicit timeout on the Payments call, based on how it normally behaves: if its p99 is 300 ms, waiting 800 ms covers healthy slow calls while cutting off sick ones.
Checkouts that hit the timeout fail — but they fail in under a second, threads come back, and the rest of Orders keeps working.

card.title: Choosing a timeout
lines: Payments p99 on a good day: 300 ms
= a stuck call frees its thread fast

steps.title: Most blips go away
body: The database recovers. Now a different pattern shows up: about one call in 50 fails for passing reasons — a pod restarting, a dropped connection. Those are transient failures, and an immediate second try almost always works.
One retry lifts success from 98% to 99.5% for a few percent more load. Retrying is only safe because the charge carries an idempotency key — a repeated charge can't bill twice.

card.title: Transient failures
lines: a restarted pod, a dropped packet

steps.title: Retries pile on a struggling service
body: Friday at 6 pm Payments gets busy and starts failing some calls. Orders retries each failure three times, instantly. The phone app also retries failed checkouts. Payments, already overloaded, now gets four times the traffic — and fails even more.
This retry storm feeds itself: the more it fails, the more it's retried. Retries that help with blips make real overload much worse.

card.title: Retry storm
lines: ! the app retries too: worst case 4 × 4 = 16×
# retries hit hardest exactly when it's down

steps.title: Wait longer, and not all together
body: Exponential backoff doubles the wait before each attempt (100, 200, 400 ms…), giving a struggling service room to recover. Jitter randomises each wait so thousands of clients don't retry in the same millisecond.
Add a cap (at most 3 tries) and a retry budget (retries may add at most 10% extra load), and retry in one layer only — not in the app, Orders and Payments all at once.

card.title: When do retries land?
lines: # cap tries at 3; retry budget ≤ 10% extra

steps.title: Stop calling, for a while
body: When Payments is clearly down, even careful retries waste time. A circuit breaker in Orders watches recent results; once most calls fail, it opens and fails every call instantly without touching the network.
After a cool-down it goes half-open and lets a few trial calls through. If they succeed, it closes and traffic resumes; if not, it waits again. Payments gets quiet time to recover.

card.title: Circuit breaker
lines: OPEN: fail instantly, no call for 30 s
HALF-OPEN: let a few trial calls through
trials pass → CLOSED · fail → OPEN again

steps.title: A worse answer beats no answer
body: Failing fast protects the system, but the shopper still sees an error. A fallback gives a degraded but useful result instead: accept the order, queue the charge, and confirm by email once Payments is back (with limits for new customers to manage fraud risk).
If Picks is down, show cached bestsellers. Every dependency deserves the question: what's good enough when it's gone?

card.title: Degrade, don't die
lines: queue the charge, confirm by email
# decide per feature: what's good enough?

steps.title: Watertight compartments
body: Now Picks hangs for 5 seconds per call. Suggestions are optional, but with one shared thread pool, slow Picks calls slowly take all 200 threads and checkout starves — a nice-to-have breaking a must-have.
Bulkheads give each dependency its own limited pool (or concurrency limit): Picks may use 30 threads, Payments 120. When Picks is slow, only its compartment floods.

steps.title: Time budgets flow downstream
body: Timeouts must fit inside each other. If the app gives up at 3 s, Orders has about 2.5 s, so its Payments call can take at most 800 ms twice. Passing a deadline with each request lets every service stop work nobody is waiting for any more.
Together: timeouts bound waiting, backoff and budgets bound retries, breakers stop hopeless calls, fallbacks keep value, bulkheads contain damage.

card.title: Budgets flow downstream
lines: ! work after the caller gave up is waste
# retry in one layer only, and only idempotent calls

steps.title: Fail fast, fail small
body:
• Every remote call needs a timeout based on its normal latency.
  • Retry transient failures — with exponential backoff, jitter, a cap and idempotency.
  • Retry storms turn overload into collapse; retry in one layer only.
  • Circuit breakers stop calling a failing service and probe for recovery.
  • Fallbacks give a degraded answer; bulkheads keep one slow dependency from taking every thread.
